narrative:
The model predicted a 62.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank near the middle of their class. Your first-year ranking, also in the bottom decile compared with an average around 6 among accepted applicants, added further weight toward a negative outcome.

Your LSAT score of 39 worked in the opposite direction. It is slightly above the average of 37.2 for accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction modestly toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your low class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.7, also below the accepted average of 3.23, added some additional concern, though it was less influential than the two decile measures.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and class standing in the coming year. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can increase your score further, and look for structured bar-prep resources that have helped students with similar profiles succeed on their second attempt. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to the current rejection.
